In other words, how and why can a human being speak of his “I,” and more generally utter the word “I” meaningfully at all?

And since Phenomenology must above all turn its own author into a philosopher—that is, into the future author of systematic philosophy—the final question it must teach us to ask concerns that author himself.
At the end of his book, he must be able to answer the question:

Why does he regard himself as capable of beginning a new systematic philosophy—a philosophy intended to systematize all the true knowledge of concrete reality that is possible in this particular historical age?
And clearly, the answer to this final phenomenological question is the Phenomenology itself.

The author can regard himself as a philosopher in the strict sense—as someone capable of writing a philosophical system—only if he regards himself as having reached the highest possible degree of self-awareness.
But Phenomenology is precisely what is supposed to create this self-awareness in him.

He therefore considers himself capable of doing what he is about to do because he has actually done what he has already done: he has written this Phenomenology, whose first question concerns the “I” and whose final question, as we have just seen, concerns its own author.
In other words, Phenomenology must set itself the task of showing that every question about the human being that can be asked in our age is asked within it.

By showing this, it also shows that its author—and its reader—has attained complete self-awareness and can therefore hope to answer every question it raises. He can become a philosopher: the author who, on the basis of this Phenomenology, writes a systematic Philosophy.
Phenomenology thus proves itself to be the true and necessary introduction to philosophy. In doing so, it justifies its own existence.
But if Phenomenology must teach us to ask every possible question about the human being, then it must also teach us to question everything that had previously passed for truth.

This means that it must teach both its author and its reader to free themselves from the authority of every kind of “authority,” not merely from those authorities from which philosophy has always urged us to free ourselves.
Obviously, someone seeking philosophical knowledge cannot give up the right to doubt or critically examine something presented to him as a “truth” of supposedly “divine” origin.
But it is equally obvious that he must not simply submit to purely human “authorities” either. He must not regard something as true solely because Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, Hegel, or Stalin said it.
The greatest danger, however, does not come from these “human” authorities. It comes from the authority of supposed “facts,” especially facts said to have been “established by science.”
Here Phenomenology must show that “facts” in the ordinary sense do not exist.

What we call a “fact” is actually the result of an interaction between human consciousness and a reality independent of that consciousness. A “fact” therefore always contains not only reality itself but also a theory of that reality—and that theory may well be false.
Moreover, this theory is shaped not only by natural reality but also by the social and political conditions under which the human being who establishes the “fact” exists.
In short, Phenomenology must teach us to see in so-called “facts” the same class ideologies that we recognize more openly in “theories.”
It must show how and why these ideologies arise, disappear, and change, and how, along with them, not only certain theories but many supposed “facts” arise, disappear, and change as well.
Something regarded as a fact under “theory A” may, after the appearance of a new “theory B,” cease to count as a fact and instead be seen as a false theoretical assumption built into the old theory.

The supporter of “theory B” may think that he has established a new fact and refuted an old theory. For the phenomenologist, however, what has happened is that one ideology has replaced another, producing corresponding changes in what counts as theory and what counts as fact.
And when the “fact” concerns not nature but the human world, the issue becomes still more delicate.
With a change of ideology, what changes is not merely what people regard as a fact. What is actually a fact can itself change.
For when ideologies change, the human world itself changes—or, more exactly, ideology changes in response to a real historical transformation.
Something that really was a fact while theory A existed can therefore cease to be a fact when theory B appears.
Theory B may think that it has corrected a theoretical error in “theory A.” The phenomenologist, by contrast, must show that the fact itself has in reality changed.
Phenomenology therefore does not, of course, deny that there is a fundamental distinction between fact and theory. It is very far from any form of “idealism.”
But at the outset it calls into question, in exactly the same way, both what presents itself as a true theory and what presents itself as a fact.

Ignoring divine authorities, human authorities, and the authority of “facts,” Phenomenology must treat the whole body of knowledge accumulated by humanity throughout its history as a succession of ideologies, each replacing another and each corresponding to humanity in a particular historical form.

Where these ideologies include theories and “facts” concerning the natural world, Phenomenology will accept as fact and true theory only what has been established through experimental and technical verification.
Where theories and facts concern the human world, it will take seriously only what has survived revolutionary verification.

Everything else is, for Phenomenology, neither a fact nor a theory, whether true or false. It is an ideology. And an ideology is not something simply to accept or refute, but something to understand as an ideology, in accordance with the regularity and inner logic that make it what it is.
In this sense, we can apply to Phenomenology Lenin’s remark about Tolstoy: its aim is to “tear away every kind of mask.”

Behind the mask of the “objective truth” of an unverified fact, Phenomenology must uncover temporary social and political interests and understand why they arose, why they changed, and why they disappeared.
Once “truths” and “facts” have been subjected to this critical treatment, most of them will prove to have been theoretical errors.
In one sense, then, we could give Phenomenology the subtitle “A History of Humanity’s Errors.”
But although Phenomenology studies false knowledge precisely as false, its own knowledge of that false knowledge is itself true: it knows that what it is studying consists of errors.
A true phenomenological knowledge of false knowledge is absolutely necessary if we are to reach true philosophical knowledge of concrete reality.
Phenomenology studies ideologies—that is, ultimately, humanity’s theoretical errors.
But it does not do this out of mere curiosity. It does so because it cannot achieve its own aim—philosophical self-awareness and philosophical knowledge—without this study.
We have seen that, without revolutionary verification, there is no way to distinguish true knowledge of the human being from mere opinion. But such verification presupposes an ideological struggle.
The philosopher can therefore be sure that his knowledge is true only by knowing where it came from—that is, by knowing its ideological, or if one prefers, its erroneous, origins.
In this sense, the phenomenological study of all the errors humanity has made throughout history is a necessary condition of the search for absolute or final truth.
We reach the same conclusion if we begin from the principle that this search can succeed only when the person conducting it has reached complete self-awareness.
To be self-aware—to know oneself—is to know what the human being is.

But to know the human being fully, it is not enough to know what human beings are at one particular moment. What human beings once were is just as characteristic of humanity as what they have now become.
To know humanity, then, we must know the errors human beings are capable of making just as much as we must know the truths they are capable of discovering.

We cannot know what the human being is without knowing, for example, that in the nineteenth century some people discovered the law of conservation of energy and others laid the foundations of scientific socialism.

But it is equally impossible to know the human being while forgetting that people in, say, the thirteenth century believed the Sun revolved around the Earth and firmly believed in the “devil” and the “Immaculate Conception.”

And if the philosopher must know that, with respect to true knowledge, he is the heir of Robert Mayer and Karl Marx, he must also recognize that, in a certain sense, he is the heir of Ptolemy and, in particular, Thomas Aquinas.
He or his predecessors may have refused this inheritance. But the inheritance existed, and it is still there.

And since refusing an inheritance is not the same thing as having no inheritance, knowing the errors humanity has overcome is just as essential to true knowledge of the human being as knowing the genuine achievements inherited from the past.
To know himself completely, the philosopher must first know everything he has inherited and, second, understand why he accepts one part of that inheritance and rejects another.
Phenomenology provides him with both kinds of self-knowledge.

The phenomenologist therefore studies humanity’s errors precisely because his aim is conscious, philosophical knowledge of the truth, and because he knows that he cannot reach it without passing through the study of those errors.
In this respect, the work of the phenomenologist is identical to the work Descartes performs in the “skeptical” part of his philosophy.
In one sense, the path of Phenomenology is the “path of doubt,” or even, as Hegel adds, the “path of despair.”
It shows the philosopher how theories that throughout history were regarded as true, even as “self-evident,” eventually die, and how seemingly unshakable “facts” evaporate.
Seeing this, the philosopher learns to doubt every “truth” and every “fact” familiar to him, and to see them as the “ideological masks” of human “interests.”
This spectacle could indeed drive him to despair if he did not at the same time see that the destructive process follows a regular pattern.
It is this regularity that makes the process intelligible and provides the knowledge that makes true knowledge possible.

The same is true of Descartes. He looked for reasons to doubt everything that appeared true to him, and everything others presented to him as true, not because he wanted to doubt forever, but because he wanted to discover what could survive every possible doubt.

There is only one difference. Descartes hoped to travel the path of doubt alone. The phenomenologist knows that, in order to travel it, he must study an ongoing historical process that exists independently of him.
In this sense, Phenomenology resembles the dialectical part of Plato’s philosophy: his Dialogues.
There the philosopher observes the same principle in the confrontation between different human opinions.
At first sight, it can appear that all we are seeing is the mutual destruction of different “truths” and “facts.”

But in reality, just as in Phenomenology, the regular pattern through which the opinions destroy one another gives rise to genuine knowledge. The observer understands the regularity at work, draws true knowledge from it, and in this way becomes a systematic philosopher.

Both of the conflicting opinions disappear. But their mutually determined destruction produces a true knowledge that is no longer subject to dialectical destruction and can therefore pass from the Dialogues into systematic philosophy.

Exactly the same is true of ideologies. Their mutual destruction produces the “philosophical” truth that reveals concrete reality as a whole instead of merely reflecting the one-sided “interests” of particular groups of human beings.

The only difference is that in Plato the dialectic of “opinions” takes the form of a peaceful conversation, whereas the dialectic of ideologies observed by the phenomenologist can sometimes take the form of a bloody struggle.
The phenomenologist must not ignore the dialectic of “conversations,” however.
In particular, he must study the philosophical aspects of ideologies.

In this sense, Phenomenology plays, in relation to systematic philosophy, the same role as a historical introduction to philosophy, in which knowledge of philosophy’s past is supposed to help us understand its present and thereby reveal the possibility of its further development.
The difference is that Phenomenology sees the philosophies it studies as aspects of the broader social ideologies to which they correspond.

It therefore discovers a meaningful order and a regular development where an ordinary historian of philosophy sees only a contingent collection of philosophical opinions that contradict and exclude one another.
But doubting ideologies and dialectically destroying them is still not enough to attain self-conscious knowledge, that is, philosophical knowledge.
To know clearly that one possesses true knowledge, one must be able to distinguish knowledge from opinion and truth from ideology.
For this, it is not enough to know what an opinion refuted by doubt is, or what a socially conditioned ideology is—an ideology that can therefore be socially destroyed.
One must also know what true knowledge itself consists in.
And insofar as the character of true knowledge—its distinguishing features—can be defined before one actually possesses it, Phenomenology is required to provide this definition.
Only by learning these features from Phenomenology can the philosopher genuinely know that the knowledge he possesses is true.
And since it is impossible to possess true knowledge without knowing what true knowledge is, Phenomenology is, in this respect too, a necessary precondition of philosophy.
We can say that the “absolute” knowledge toward which philosophy strives—that is, final or perfect knowledge—becomes possible when the totality of human opinions coincides with complete truth.
But to understand what this means, we first have to clarify the words involved.
Ordinarily, when we speak of opinion, we add the adjective “subjective.” When we speak of “truth,” by contrast, we call it “objective.”
When we are dealing with an opinion or an ideology, it matters a great deal who holds that opinion and whose interests the ideology expresses.
But when we are dealing with truth, these questions about persons cease to matter.
